strengths: Introduces a simple, parameter-free technique for KV cache compression based on DCT low-pass filtering, motivated by an interesting empirical observation of energy concentration in low-frequency components across LLaMA-2 decoder layers.
The approach avoids adding extra modules/parameters (unlike LoCoCo or Activation Beacon), which improves practicality and ease of integration with existing LLM architectures.

Fairly comprehensive empirical study covering both language modeling (PPL on PG-19/Proof-pile) and downstream long-context understanding (LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack), with comparisons against multiple relevant baselines (LongLoRA, LoCoCo, SnapKV, PyramidKV, LM-Infinite, LongHeads).
Efficiency analysis (decoding latency, FLOPs breakdown, compression overhead) is thorough and demonstrates the method's near-linear scaling and negligible compression overhead.

Useful ablations in the appendix, including retaining ratio sensitivity, head-wise power spectrum analysis, and the RoPE-before-vs-after compression comparison, which help substantiate design choices.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it is essentially a low-pass frequency-domain smoothing/downsampling of cached representations, conceptually adjacent to existing merging/compression techniques (e.g., CaM, D2O) and to prior frequency-domain works (Fourier Transformer, FNet), and the paper does not strongly demonstrate why DCT compression is fundamentally better than simpler pooling/merging approaches beyond a single 'Dropping' baseline comparison.

The motivating power spectrum analysis (Figure 1) is computed over full, non-causal sequences, which does not directly justify why iteratively re-compressing partial, growing, autoregressively-generated caches preserves relevant information for future token prediction; this gap between the analysis and the actual iterative algorithm is not rigorously addressed.

Results on LongBench (Table 2) are mixed: FreqKV underperforms the base uncompressed model and other baselines on several sub-tasks (e.g., Qasper, MF-en, TREC, RB-P), which somewhat undercuts the 'consistently improves' claim, and the paper does not analyze why the method fails on some categories.

The very strong NIAH results (FreqKV outperforming the full-context, uncompressed LLaMA-2-chat baseline in Table 2's implied comparison, and much higher NIAH accuracy than PyramidKV) are not well explained given that the method is inherently lossy; there is no discussion of variance, multiple seeds, or the possibility that retrieval tasks benefit disproportionately from the specific sink+low-frequency retention scheme, leaving the strong results somewhat unconvincing without deeper analysis.

Missing comparisons: LoCoCo and Activation Beacon are not evaluated on LongBench/NIAH tasks, and no comparison is made against more recent/strong context-extension baselines beyond 7B/8B scale, limiting the generality and significance of the conclusions.

Iterative repeated compression (compressing already-compressed representations together with new tokens) could compound reconstruction error over many iterations, but the paper provides no analysis of degradation as compression count grows beyond aggregate PPL curves at very long context (e.g., no probing of information loss for very early tokens after 15+ compression iterations).

Reproducibility details are limited: no mention of code release, and hyperparameter/training details (e.g., how retaining ratio interacts across different model architectures like GQA in LLaMA-3) are only briefly covered.

strengths: Novel and simple idea: applying DCT-based low-pass filtering to compress KV cache in the frequency domain for decoder-only LLMs, motivated by a clear empirical observation (energy concentration in low-frequency components) shown via power spectrum analysis across layers.

Parameter-free/architecture-free method: no additional trainable modules are introduced, unlike LoCoCo or Activation Beacon, making the method lightweight and easy to integrate with minimal fine-tuning (LoRA).

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation across long-context language modeling (PG-19, Proof-pile) and long-context understanding (LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack), and across two model families (LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3).

Good set of ablations and analyses: retaining ratio sensitivity, head-wise power spectrum patterns, a 'Dropping' baseline to isolate the benefit of frequency-domain compression versus simple recency-based eviction, and a RoPE-compression variant showing why compressing key states before RoPE is important.

Efficiency claims are backed by concrete decoding latency and FLOPs measurements, showing the compression overhead is negligible (<0.5%) while enabling near-linear decoding time versus quadratic growth for full-cache attention.
The method extends context length considerably beyond training length (8K training to 64K evaluation) with stable perplexity, which is a meaningful practical benefit.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to 7B/8B scale models; no validation at larger model scales or across model families beyond LLaMA, which limits confidence in generality.

LongBench results are mixed at the per-task level (FreqKV underperforms strong baselines like SnapKV/PyramidKV on several individual tasks such as MF-en, TREC, LCC), and the paper does not deeply analyze why frequency compression helps/hurts specific task types beyond a brief note on Proof-pile.

The retaining ratio and sink size are fixed globally and heuristically chosen (γ=0.5, S=4), despite the paper's own head-wise/layer-wise analysis showing that energy concentration varies noticeably across layers and heads; an adaptive or layer/head-specific compression ratio is not explored, which seems like a natural and possibly impactful extension left unaddressed.

The theoretical justification remains largely empirical/heuristic (power spectrum energy concentration), without deeper analysis connecting DCT low-pass filtering to attention output fidelity or providing bounds/guarantees on information loss.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat inconsistent across tables: Activation Beacon and Landmark Attention, discussed extensively in related work as key competitors, are not included in the main quantitative comparisons (Tables 1 and 2), and LoCoCo is only reproduced by the authors rather than using official reported numbers, raising reproducibility concerns.

The performance gains over strong full-KV baselines (e.g., Full FT, LongLoRA) on Proof-pile are notably worse at longer context lengths, suggesting the method's benefits may not generalize as well to more structured/technical text domains.

The paper claims 'comparable performance' to full KV cache methods in several places, but some comparisons (e.g., against Full FT with much larger training length) are not fully controlled, making it harder to isolate the exact source of gains (compression scheme vs. training procedure differences).

strengths: Novel and reasonably well-motivated idea: framing KV cache redundancy reduction as a frequency-domain (DCT) low-pass filtering problem for decoder-only LLMs, which to the authors' knowledge has not been explored before for autoregressive KV compression.

Solid empirical motivation: power spectrum analysis across layers/heads, targeted perturbation experiments, and summarization ablations converge on a consistent story that low-frequency components carry global/semantic information while high-frequency components carry local detail.

The method is parameter-free and architecture-agnostic, avoiding the extra memory overhead of learned compressor modules (e.g., Activation Beacon, LoCoCo), and integrates cleanly with RoPE by compressing before rotary encoding and reassigning cache-local position indices, avoiding out-of-window position extrapolation issues.

Broad and fairly rigorous experimental coverage: perplexity on PG-19/Proof-pile up to 256K context, LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongGenBench, spanning both prefilling/understanding and decoding/generation scenarios.

Extensive ablations (retaining ratio, sink size, high- vs low-frequency retention, RoPE-before/after compression, rescaling factor, dropping-vs-compression variant) that support the design choices and add credibility to the core claims.
Efficiency analysis is thorough: near-linear decoding latency, negligible FLOPs/time overhead from the compression step (<0.5%), and notable reduction in training time/memory versus full fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Potentially unfair comparison protocol: most eviction/merging baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, GemFilter, D2O, etc.) are applied training-free to the base model, whereas FreqKV benefits from additional LongAlpaca SFT specifically tuned for the compression/extension mechanism, confounding the source of the reported gains.

Key related methods explicitly designed for context extension with compression (LoCoCo, Activation Beacon) are only evaluated on perplexity (Table 2/9) and excluded from the main downstream understanding/generation benchmarks (LongBench, RULER, NIAH, LongGenBench), leaving the strongest and most comparable competitors untested on the tasks that matter most for the paper's claims.

Despite claims of robustness at extended lengths, absolute performance at 16K on RULER (47.3 average) remains quite low relative to in-window performance (87.68 at 8K), suggesting substantial degradation is merely less catastrophic than baselines rather than genuinely strong.

Mixed results on LongBench: FreqKV is not uniformly best across tasks (e.g., noticeably worse than PyramidKV/SnapKV on TREC, RB-P for LLaMA-2, and few-shot learning tasks), and improvements on other metrics are sometimes marginal, weakening the 'consistently outperforms' claim.

The core mechanism (retaining low-frequency DCT components) is conceptually close to a smoothing/averaging operation, and its relationship/advantage over simpler token-merging approaches (CaM, KVMerger) is not deeply analyzed beyond aggregate benchmark scores.

No wall-clock or memory comparison against baselines during actual prefilling on long-context benchmarks (only decoding latency and FLOPs are profiled), leaving prefilling-stage efficiency claims less substantiated.

The Proof-pile results show FreqKV underperforming LongLoRA (full-cache) at longer lengths, indicating information loss for symbol-dense content, which somewhat undercuts the 'preserves all information' framing of the method.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting DCT-based frequency-domain energy concentration for KV cache compression in decoder-only LLMs is a reasonably novel angle relative to prior eviction/merging-based KV compression methods.
The method is parameter-free and architecture-agnostic, requiring only minimal fine-tuning (8K length) to extend context to very long lengths (up to 256K), which is an attractive practical property.

Broad experimental coverage: language modeling (PG-19, Proof-pile), long-context understanding (LongBench, RULER, NIAH), and long-generation (LongGenBench), compared against a large number of recent strong baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, GemFilter, D2O, CaM, KVMerger, ThinK, LaCache, LoCoCo, LongLoRA).

Reasonably thorough ablations on retaining ratio, sink size, high/low frequency retention, rescaling factor, and RoPE placement, plus efficiency/FLOPs/latency analysis showing negligible compression overhead.
The design of compressing key states before RoPE application to avoid out-of-distribution position indices is a sensible and seemingly effective engineering choice.
weaknesses: The central empirical motivation (low-frequency = global/semantic, high-frequency = local/detail) rests on a small-scale, somewhat ad hoc perturbation experiment (100 documents, 1% synonym replacement) and a single summarization-task comparison; this evidence is suggestive but not rigorous enough to fully support the strong causal framing used throughout the paper.

The method still discards information (high-frequency components), so the claim of 'preserving the information of all tokens' versus eviction methods is overstated — the compression is lossy in a different way, not lossless, and the paper does not clearly quantify how much true information is retained versus eviction beyond downstream task scores.

At aggressive compression (1% retaining ratio) or long extrapolated lengths beyond training, gains over strong baselines (e.g., PyramidKV) are often marginal (e.g., LongBench avg 35.54 vs 35.10 for LLaMA-2), undermining the claim of consistently large improvements.

On RULER at 16K, FreqKV's performance collapses substantially from 8K (87.68 → 47.30 avg), which, while better than baselines' near-total failure, still indicates the method does not robustly solve long-range extrapolation and raises concern about how meaningful the 'context window extension' claim is in practice.

On Proof-pile, FreqKV underperforms LongLoRA (which uses full, uncompressed cache) at longer lengths, indicating the frequency-domain compression struggles with dense symbolic/mathematical content, which is a notable limitation not sufficiently addressed.

Baseline comparisons for KV-cache eviction/merging methods are reproduced by the authors using official code, but details on hyperparameter tuning fairness (e.g., whether all methods received comparable training/tuning budgets) are not fully transparent, raising some reproducibility/fairness concerns.

The paper does not compare against strong RoPE-scaling/position-extrapolation methods (e.g., LongRoPE, YaRN, NTK-aware scaling) in the main experimental tables, despite mentioning them in related work, leaving open how FreqKV compares to that alternative and arguably more established line of context-extension work.

The novelty is somewhat incremental given the substantial prior literature on frequency-domain processing in deep learning (FNet, Fourier Transformer, Frequency Principle) — the main contribution is largely an application/adaptation of known DCT low-pass filtering ideas to the decoder-only KV cache setting, rather than a fundamentally new technique.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: exploiting energy concentration of KV states in the low-frequency DCT domain, with clear empirical support (power spectrum analysis, perturbation robustness study, and summarization ablation) that ties directly into the method design.

First systematic exploration of frequency-domain KV compression tailored to the causal, autoregressive nature of decoder-only LLMs, addressed via chunk-wise iterative compression with uncompressed sink tokens, which elegantly aligns with attention-sink findings.
Parameter-free and architecture-agnostic design that avoids the extra memory/parameter overhead of methods like Activation Beacon or LoCoCo.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning language modeling (PG-19, Proof-pile), long-context understanding (LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack), and long-context generation (LongGenBench), across LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3 and multiple model sizes.

Impressive extrapolation results: training at 8K but maintaining stable perplexity up to 256K, with negligible (<0.3%) compression latency overhead, along with reduced training time/memory versus full fine-tuning.

Thorough set of ablations (retaining ratio, sink size, high- vs low-frequency retention, RoPE-before/after-compression, rescaling factor, FLOPs/latency overhead) that substantiate design choices and improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Some baseline comparisons are not entirely apples-to-apples: many eviction/merging baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, D2O, etc.) are training-free, whereas FreqKV benefits from additional LoRA fine-tuning at the target context length, which could partly explain performance gaps, especially at extended lengths beyond the original window.

On Proof-pile, FreqKV underperforms LongLoRA (which retains the full cache) at longer context lengths, indicating that the compression can lose fidelity for dense symbolic/mathematical content — a limitation only partially discussed.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental in that DCT-based low-pass filtering for sequence compression has precedent in vision/CNN compression and encoder-only NLP models (FNet, Fourier Transformer); the main contribution here is largely the causal/iterative adaptation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Limited theoretical analysis of how repeated (iterative) lossy compression across many steps affects information retention/error accumulation over very long sequences beyond the empirical perplexity curves; deeper analysis of failure modes would strengthen claims of robustness.

Comparisons on LongBench/RULER/NIAH omit some of the paper's own related-work baselines (e.g., LoCoCo, Activation Beacon) that are only evaluated on PPL, leaving the full picture of relative performance versus additional-parameter compressors incomplete.
Evaluation is restricted to LLaMA-2/LLaMA-3 family; the method's generality across other architectures (e.g., other GQA/MQA-heavy models, other position encoding schemes) is not demonstrated.
